segments.say: Lesson 3. What Happens When You Hit Enter. D N S, T C P/T L S, H T T P, C D N, load balancer, app server, database: the request lifecycle end to end.

When you open a website, your request passes through D N S, a C D N, a load balancer, an app server, a cache and a database. Knowing that path is the foundation of every design. Here is an analogy. Posting a letter: look up the address (D N S), drop it at the nearest post office (C D N / load balancer), it's routed to the right department (server), which checks its files (cache/D B) and replies.

Why does this matter? "What happens when you type a U R L?" is a classic opener. Every later design builds on this request path. A few key words. D N S: Turns domain names into I P addresses. T L S: Encryption that makes H T T P into H T T P S. C D N: Servers near users that cache static files. Latency: Time for one request to complete.
Request lifecycle. You type shop.example.com. The browser first needs an I P address.
D N S resolves the name (browser cache leads to O S leads to resolver leads to root leads to T L D leads to authoritative). Answers are cached for their T T L. D N S can also do geo-routing.
Static assets (J S, C S S, images) come from a C D N edge near the user, which is fast and offloads origin servers.
The A P I call opens T C P plus T L S (H T T P S) to the load balancer, which picks a healthy app server.
A stateless app server handles the request (sessions live in a shared store, so any server can serve any user).
Check the cache first. A hit costs ~1 ms.
On a miss, query the database, then populate the cache.
Response travels back as H T T P status plus headers plus jason body. Every box here is a topic in this track.

Key pieces. D N S: name leads to I P. Hierarchical and cached. T T L controls how fast changes propagate. T C P plus T L S: reliable connection plus encryption. H T T P/2 multiplexes requests; H T T P/3 runs on Q U I C (U D P). H T T P: methods (G E T, P O S T, P U T, P A T C H, DELETE), status codes (2xx ok, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error), headers (cache-control, auth). C D N: caches content at edge locations close to users.

Latency numbers to remember (roughly). L1 cache ~1 ns, R A M ~100 ns. S S D random read ~100 µs. Same-datacenter round trip ~0.5 ms. Redis G E T ~<1 ms, simple D B query ~1–10 ms. Cross-continent round trip ~100–150 ms. Takeaway: network hops and disk dominate, so cache close to the user and avoid chatty calls.

Say it in the interview. "D N S resolves the domain, static assets come from a C D N, and A P I calls hit a load balancer that terminates T L S and routes to stateless app servers. They read through a cache to the database. That's the baseline I'd start from and then scale each layer.".

H T T P status codes you must know. 200 / 201: OK / Created, success; P O S T created a resource. 204: No Content, successful DELETE. 301 / 302: Moved permanently / temporarily, redirects (U R L shortener!). 304: Not Modified, client cache still valid. 400 / 401 / 403 / 404: Bad request / Unauthenticated / Forbidden / Not found, client errors. 409: Conflict, version conflict, duplicate. 429: Too Many Requests, rate limiting. 500 / 502 / 503 / 504: Server error / Bad gateway / Unavailable / Gateway timeout, server-side failures.

A likely interview question: What happens when you type a U R L and press enter? A strong answer: D N S resolution, T C P and T L S handshake, H T T P request to the C D N (static) or load balancer (A P I), L B routes to a stateless app server, app checks cache then D B, response returns and the browser renders and fetches sub-resources.
That's it for What Happens When You Hit Enter. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
